title: The Interest-Only Cliff: The Loan Repayment Jump Most SME Owners Don't See Coming
excerpt: Interest-only terms on business loans are set up to protect cash flow during growth. When the period ends, repayments step up hard, and the gap is rarely modelled in advance.
content:
Somewhere in the facility paperwork from two or three years ago sits a date that matters more than almost anything else in the business right now. It is the date the interest-only period on a loan rolls off and the repayments switch to principal and interest. Most owners could not tell you that date without checking.

That is not a criticism. Interest-only terms are usually negotiated once, at settlement, and then the facility becomes background noise. The direct debit comes out, the balance sheet looks steady, and attention moves on to running the business. The trouble is that the repayment on that same facility can step up meaningfully the moment the interest-only period ends, because the loan now has to repay principal over whatever term is left, not the original term. The business has not changed. The repayment has.

For East Coast businesses that borrowed to fund a fit-out, equipment, or a property purchase during a growth run in the last few years, this is a live issue right now, not a future one.

Why Interest-Only Felt Like the Right Call at the Time

There was nothing wrong with the original decision. Interest-only structuring is a sensible way to protect cash during a phase when a business is investing ahead of revenue, whether that is a second site, a fleet upgrade, or new equipment that takes a year or two to earn its keep. Keeping repayments to interest alone during that window is exactly the kind of deliberate trade-off a growing business should make.

The pattern we see is not that the decision was wrong. It is that the decision was made once and never revisited. The interest-only period was a feature of the deal at the time it was signed, not a permanent setting. Most business lenders write interest-only terms for one to five years, and the step-up at the end is built into the loan from day one, even if nobody has looked at it since.

What Actually Changes When the Period Ends

Two things happen at once, and both push in the same direction. First, the repayment has to start covering principal, and because the remaining term is shorter than the original term, that principal gets compressed into fewer years than the business might expect. Second, many lenders reassess the facility at the point of conversion, pricing it at current rates rather than the rate that applied at settlement. A facility that felt comfortable at origination can land quite differently once both of those factors move together.

The businesses that feel this hardest are usually the ones where the original loan was sized against a cash flow position from a few years ago, one that has since shifted, whether through new debt taken on elsewhere, a change in trading terms, or simply a leaner margin than when the facility was approved. None of that shows up until the new repayment actually lands. A working cash flow discipline habit built around a 13-week view would have flagged the gap months earlier. Without it, the first signal is often the bank statement itself.

The Review Worth Running Before the Step-Up Hits

The fix is not complicated, but it does need to happen before the conversion date, not after. It starts with pulling every facility the business holds and listing the interest-only expiry date against each one, because businesses that have borrowed more than once often have staggered dates sitting across different lenders. From there, the new principal and interest repayment can be modelled against current cash flow, at current rates, not the rates assumed when the loan was approved.

If the modelled repayment is tight, there are genuine options worth putting to the lender well ahead of the deadline: extending the interest-only term, restructuring the facility across a longer period, consolidating multiple facilities into one, or refinancing to a lender whose terms better match where the business is now rather than where it was when the loan was written. This is precisely the territory a Banking and Facility Review is built for, an independent look at existing facilities, covenants and pricing that is designed to surface exactly this kind of step-up before it arrives as a surprise.

None of this requires a crisis to justify the conversation. It is simply the kind of forward check that an owner running the business day to day rarely has the vantage point to run alone, which is part of why an ongoing fractional CFO relationship tends to catch these dates as a matter of course rather than after the fact. The businesses that come through a step-up calmly are almost always the ones that saw the date coming on a calendar, not the ones that saw it coming on a bank statement.

faqs.q: What does interest-only mean on a business loan in Australia?
faqs.a: It means the repayment only covers the interest charged each period, with none of it reducing the original loan balance. Lenders typically offer this for one to five years on business loans, often to support cash flow during a growth phase, a fit-out or an equipment purchase. Once the period ends, the loan converts to principal and interest repayments.

faqs.q: How much do repayments increase when a loan moves to principal and interest?
faqs.a: It depends on the balance, the rate and how much term is left once the interest-only period ends, but the jump is usually noticeable because the full balance now has to be repaid over a shorter remaining term than the loan originally had. Modelling the new figure against current cash flow, ideally through a Banking and Facility Review, avoids the number arriving as a surprise.

faqs.q: Can you extend the interest-only period on an existing business loan?
faqs.a: Often, yes, though it is a conversation to raise with the lender well before the current period expires rather than after. Lenders will usually want an updated view of trading performance and serviceability before agreeing, which is easier to present when the business has current financials and a clear cash flow position ready to go.

faqs.q: How do I find out when my business loan's interest-only period ends?
faqs.a: The expiry date sits in the original facility letter or loan contract, and it is worth checking directly with the lender if that paperwork is not easy to locate, since the date will not usually be flagged again before it arrives. Businesses holding more than one facility often find the dates are staggered across different lenders.

faqs.q: What should a business do if it cannot afford the higher repayment after interest-only ends?
faqs.a: Raise it with the lender before the conversion date, not after, because refinancing, restructuring or extending the interest-only term are all easier to negotiate ahead of time than once a repayment has already been missed. A cash flow discipline approach that forecasts the new figure gives enough runway to act on it properly.

faqs.q: Does a bank reassess serviceability when an interest-only period expires?
faqs.a: Many lenders do reassess the facility at conversion, pricing it against current rates and current financials rather than the terms that applied when the loan was first approved. That is one reason a facility that felt comfortable at settlement can land differently a few years later, even if the business itself has not changed much.

faqs.q: Is refinancing worth considering before an interest-only period ends?
faqs.a: It is worth comparing at minimum, because a facility structured for the business as it was two or three years ago is not always the best fit for the business today. An independent review of existing facilities against current terms, rather than simply accepting the lender's default conversion, is the kind of check worth running on a fixed cadence, not just once at settlement.
